item.title: Craig Carton blasts Michigan fans for storming field after controversial win: 'They’re a bunch of morons'
item.description: Craig Carton ripped Michigan fans for storming the field after Bryce Underwood's controversial Hail Mary barely beat Western Michigan 13-12.
item.content:encoded:
Craig Carton scorched Michigan Wolverines fans for celebrating the team’s controversial victory against the Western Michigan Broncos on Saturday night.

There’s no argument that Michigan needed a little bit of luck to get past Western Michigan 13-12. Bryce Underwood received a second Hail Mary opportunity as officials determined that a Western Michigan defended touched his first throw in the final moments with one second left on the clock. Underwood found J.J. Buchanan for the game-winning score.

Is that a real reason to storm the field and act like you beat Ohio State? An emphatic no, says Carton, whose "Craig Carton Show" premieres on OutKick on Tuesday. Carton put it better than I could.

CRAIG CARTON: I'M BRINGING MY 'UNWAVERING, UNAPOLOGETIC' OPINIONS TO OUTKICK

"The thing that bothers me more than the hubris of adding a second to the game and giving Michigan another opportunity to win that game was the fact that there was 110,000 people at Michigan for that game and at the end of the game they stormed the field like they were Western Michigan knocking off a Big Ten team on the road," Carton said. "And it just was a good reminder to me that even though Michigan is thought of as a top educational experience for the kids that take the six years they normally take to graduate, the reality is that they’re a bunch of morons.

"Now, we already know that Michigan is a corrupt athletic program. We know that it’s a dirty athletic program. We know that coaches like to sleep with coeds there. Coaches like to steal signs there. Coaches like to cheat there. But what I didn’t know as a fact until Saturday night is that that 18-27 year olds that call Michigan their undergraduate home are morons. The fact that you would storm the field when barely beating and, let’s be honest, needing the Big Ten to cheat for you to win the game, the fact that you would storm the field when you won by a single point because you were given an extra second of time while 27-point favorites tells me everything I need to know about the type of kid that goes to Michigan."

SUBSCRIBE TO 'THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW' ON YOUTUBE

Remember, it’s not as though Michigan was unranked (they were 16th going into Saturday) and were up against Ohio State or Texas or Alabama or Oregon or even Rutgers for that matter.

The Wolverines were playing Western Michigan that plays in the Mid-American Conference and have been an FBS program since 1962. The Broncos have never beaten an opponent inside the top 20 of the Associated Press poll.

"That’s not a game to be celebrated if you’re a Michigan fan or a Michigan alumni," Carton added. "That’s a game to give you a warning about what’s to come for the rest of this season. Michigan football is dead. Michigan football is an embarrassment. Michigan football pays their quarterback $10 million a year and I would be better.

WATCH THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW ON OUTKICK

"So, just remember what you saw Saturday night. You saw a Wolverine program that needed cheating and needed secretive clocks to beat a MAC team while favored by 27 points. And the kids there are either so drunk, so high or so stupid that they stormed the field like they had accomplished something. You didn’t accomplish a damn thing but embarrassing yourselves on Saturday night."

Western Michigan has been ranked in the AP poll once ever – that coming in 2016 when they were 13-1 under P.J. Fleck. A victory over a blue blood would have been the biggest win in the program’s history.

The Big Ten and Mid-American Conference both released statements on the clock controversy after the game, reiterating that a Broncos defender touched the ball while out of bounds with one second left.

Michigan fans’ celebration was certainly silly and they will be needled for it until the next cray thing happens.

For now, the team itself has to prepare for noon ET showdown with Oklahoma on Saturday as questions surround Underwood about his status as QB1 for the future.

Michigan and Oklahoma will battle in Ann Arbor. The game can be seen on FOX.

item.title: Smithsonian head Lonnie Bunch to retire amid allegations of far-left woke messaging at museums
item.description: Lonnie Bunch III announced his retirement from the Smithsonian Institution amid an escalating clash with the Trump administration over museum leadership.
item.content:encoded:
The head of the Smithsonian Institution announced his retirement Tuesday, stepping down amid an escalating clash with the Trump administration over the leadership and direction of the nation’s museums.

Lonnie Bunch III, who has led the Smithsonian since 2019 and was the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, said he will leave the post by the end of the year.

"It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement from the Smithsonian," Bunch said in a press release. "I have spent nearly half of my life working at and being part of the Smithsonian family, and what a privilege it has been. There is no place like the Smithsonian — it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together." 

SMITHSONIAN SHOWDOWN INTENSIFIES AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ISSUES A STARK NEW WARNING

"I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward," he added.

Bunch’s departure comes as the Trump administration has intensified scrutiny of the Smithsonian, accusing its leadership of allowing progressive ideology to shape its presentation of American history and raising concerns about potential violations of federal nondiscrimination law.

In a letter recently made public by the Department of the Interior, the administration said the Smithsonian leadership’s "institutional culture may have resulted in significant violations of Federal antidiscrimination law," including allegedly creating a hostile work environment and allocating opportunities, funding and other benefits based on race, ethnicity and other protected characteristics.

The letter did not include specific evidence of illegal activity, and the Department of the Interior did not provide further information when previously reached for comment by Fox News Digital.

The administration warned that federal agencies could withdraw certain forms of support if its concerns are not addressed, saying an "appropriate response" from the Smithsonian "must likewise address executive leadership and institutional ideology."

The pressure follows a 2025 executive order directing officials to seek the removal of what the administration called "improper ideology" from the Smithsonian.

SMITHSONIAN'S TAXPAYER FUNDS FACE CHOPPING BLOCK AS GOP DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY FOR 'WOKE' HISTORY

Bunch became the Smithsonian’s 14th secretary in June 2019, making him the first African American and first historian to hold the position. He previously led the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, serving as its founding director from 2005 through its opening in 2016.

Bunch first joined the Smithsonian in 1978 and has spent nearly four decades at the institution, apart from a period when he served as president of the Chicago Historical Society.

Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as chancellor of the Smithsonian, praised Bunch’s tenure and said the institution would work with him to ensure a smooth transition.

"From his days as a young curator at the National Air and Space and American History Museums through his tenure as the founding director of the African American History and Culture Museum and culminating in his distinguished service for the past seven years in the Smithsonian’s top job, Secretary Bunch has pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story," Roberts said.

Smithsonian Board of Regents Chair Franklin D. Raines said the board will announce an acting secretary and begin a national search for Bunch’s successor.

Fox News Digital’s Robert Schmad contributed to this report.

item.title: Families of 9/11 victims' message to Mamdani: 'Please do not come' to memorial ceremony
item.content:encoded:
A coalition of 9/11 family members, first responders, and elected officials gathered on the steps of City Hall on Tuesday to deliver a message to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani: stay away from this year's Sept. 11 memorial service.

"This mayor is not serving us," said Charles Wolf, who lost his wife on 9/11. "He's serving himself. We are asking respectfully that he not show up, even though there is going to be other politicians there. These are the politicians that helped us push beneficial laws through and literally held our hand during that time. Mayor Mamdani has not shown any of that, none of it. He just wants to be there because he wants to be there. So we are asking him to respect the fact that that trauma is revived during the ceremony. It is a private ceremony. It is not a public ceremony. Mayor Mamdani, please do not come. "

item.title: Robert Saleh and Brian Daboll aim to turn the Tennessee Titans into AFC South contenders
item.description: Robert Saleh and Brian Daboll lead a sweeping Tennessee Titans overhaul around Cam Ward, but the AFC South betting outlook hinges on key roster gaps.
item.content:encoded:
With defensive-minded head coach Robert Saleh taking over the program and veteran offensive coordinator Brian Daboll arriving to shepherd quarterback Cam Ward in his sophomore year, the Tennessee Titans are aiming to prove that its painful baseline rebuild is finally giving way to a competitive new era in the AFC South.

The Titans endured a brutal 2025 campaign, stumbling to a 3–14 finish and landing near the bottom of the league in both scoring offense and scoring defense. Rookie starter Cam Ward showed occasional dynamic flashes under pressure, while Tony Pollard provided steady work out of the backfield with a 1,082-yard rushing season. In fairness, the NFL didn’t do them many favors, giving them a really tough schedule even after a bad year. Ultimately, the lack of success on both sides of the ball led to the mid-season exit of Brian Callahan.

To reset the organization, general manager Mike Borgonzi orchestrated a sweeping offseason overhaul.

The headline moves started at the top by hiring former New York Jets head coach Robert Saleh as head coach and bringing in Brian Daboll to call plays. The problem I have is that neither has really proven successful with rebuilding teams – maybe Daboll more than Saleh.

JOSH ALLEN RECALLS HIS ROLE IN BILLS' COACHING SEARCH, DETAILS JOE BRADY’S APPROACH TO NEW ROLE

I do like teams that are intentional about upgrading areas. When you have a lot of areas to upgrade, there are only so many areas you can really make an impact. They signed former New York Giants wide receiver Wan'Dale Robinson and tight end Daniel Bellinger, added edge rusher John Franklin-Myers and defensive tackle Solomon Thomas, and bolstered the secondary with cornerbacks Alontae Taylor and Cor'Dale Flott alongside safety Tony Adams.

They also brought in veteran quarterback Mitchell Trubisky as high-end insurance. In the draft, Tennessee made massive moves by taking wideout Carnell Tate at No. 4 overall and trading back into the first round for pass rusher Keldric Faulk. Major subtractions included letting lingering free agents walk and restructuring line depth to accommodate their fresh rookie class.

The offense features a far more dynamic receiving corps with rookie Carnell Tate on the perimeter alongside Wan'Dale Robinson and Calvin Ridley, providing Ward with the quick-separation weapons he lacked as a rookie. Their line isn’t exactly top-notch, coming in at 29th for the year, but I do think there is potential they are better than they are graded at currently.

HOUSTON TEXANS' 2025 WIN TOTAL SET AT 9.5 AS CJ STROUD FACES QUESTIONS ABOUT OFFENSIVE LINE

If you plan to bet the over 6.5 wins for Tennessee, I think you attribute it to the improved weapons for Ward, the tough schedule from last season that still saw them get three wins, and the new coaching staff. If you want the under, it is looking at an offensive line that is ranked at 29th, and a defensive line ranked at 17th. The Texans have a great defense, but there are questions on that roster as well. The Colts have a quarterback coming back from an Achilles tear, and the Jaguars lost some key pieces. I have them right at six wins this year, which improves from last year, but I don’t think I can bet one way or another on them.

item.title: Alex Van Halen calls Sammy Hagar 'a complete idiot' as decades-long feud between bandmates deepens
item.description: Alex Van Halen called Sammy Hagar "a complete idiot" in a new interview, and Hagar fired back with a pointed Instagram comment over the weekend.
item.content:encoded:
Alex Van Halen has some thoughts about former bandmate Sammy Hagar.

During an interview with Brazilian music journalist Marcelo Vieira published earlier this month, Alex ripped into Hagar when asked about his 2011 memoir, "Red: My Uncensored Life in Rock."

"I don't know what he wrote, and I don't wanna know," he said, according to a translation from the original Portuguese interview published by Roadie Crew. "In my opinion, Sammy Hagar is a complete idiot."

SAMMY HAGAR BURIES DECADES-LONG FEUD WITH DAVID LEE ROTH AFTER TOUR DATES ARE AXED

Hagar has since responded to the insult, writing in an Instagram comment over the weekend, "This comment and post is so unnecessary at this time in our lives, but I guess the truth hurts sometimes. Peace already."

The latest jab comes after years of tension between the former bandmates, who have not spoken in more than two decades, according to Hagar.

ENGELBERT HUMPERDINCK MAKES BLUNT ADMISSION ABOUT MYSTERIOUS DECADES-LONG TOM JONES FEUD

A representative for Alex did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Alex previously rejected an invitation to join Hagar and former Van Halen bassist Michael Anthony for their 2024 "Best of All Worlds" tour, which celebrated Hagar's era with the band.

"I'm not interested," Alex told Billboard at the time. "They're not doing the band justice. They can do what they want to do. That's not my business."

Alex also largely focused on Van Halen's original lineup with David Lee Roth in his 2024 memoir, "Brothers," while largely omitting Hagar's decade-long run with the band.

GEORGE MICHAEL STRUGGLED WITH 'ETERNAL CONFLICT' OVER FAME, WHAM! BANDMATE ANDREW RIDGELEY SAYS

"What happened after Dave left is not the same band," Alex told Billboard while promoting the book. "I'm not saying it was better or worse or any of that.… But the magic was in the first years, when we didn't know what we were doing, when we were willing to try anything."

Earlier this year, Hagar suggested he would "never play" with Alex again more than 20 years after their last tour together.

"I'm the biggest Pink Floyd fan. I see David Gilmour say, 'I will never play with Roger Waters again,' and I know what he means," the 78-year-old told Classic Rock. "I feel that way about Alex Van Halen. They're negative people."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Hagar, who replaced Roth as lead singer of Van Halen in 1985, remained with the band until 1996. He later reunited with the group in 2004 for a reunion tour.

The singer has suggested that Alex's health problems and inability or unwillingness to continue playing drums may have contributed to the tension. Hagar speculated that Alex could be frustrated that he and Anthony continue to perform Van Halen songs while the drummer is no longer touring.

Hagar told Rolling Stone in April 2025 that he and Alex had not spoken in 21 years.

"I hate to say it, but I dreamt about Alex the other night, man," he told the magazine. "It was crazy. And it was so friggin' real. I was saying, 'What are you p---ed off at me about, man? What the f---? Now, just tell me what your problem is. What did I do? Just tell me.'"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Hagar said he thinks Alex is upset with him "because I'm out doing it, and Mike [Anthony] and I are out doing it, and he can't. He's not a singer. He's not a guitar player. He is not really a band leader. And he seems like he doesn't want to play drums or can't play drums anymore, and he can't go write a new record."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Alex wasn't the songwriter in the band," he continued. "He was the drummer. Eddie and I wrote the songs. Dave [Lee Roth] and Eddie wrote the songs, and so we can go out and do them. And I think that really bothers him that Mike and I are still out there doing it. I would feel bad. If I put myself in his shoes, I would feel terrible if I couldn't do it anymore."

Alex's criticism also follows Hagar's previous claims that he tried repeatedly to reconnect with his former bandmate, including while assembling the "Best of All Worlds" tour. Hagar said he and Anthony reached out to Alex "a dozen times" before the tour but received no response.

item.title: Adidas apologizes after ad featuring former Israeli soldier who lost leg draws boycott calls
item.description: Adidas apologized after its single shoe service campaign in Israel featuring an Israel Defense Forces veteran sparked fierce pro-Palestinian backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Adidas has issued an apology for any "offense" the company caused with its recent advertisement that featured an Israel Defense Forces veteran who lost a leg while serving.

"We recognize that an image used in a recent local activation by the local team has raised concerns and strong reactions. It was never our intent to cause offense and we apologize for anyone affected," the company said in a statement, according to The Times of Israel.

"We acknowledge the concerns that have been raised and are taking the feedback seriously."

WNBA STAR SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM'S PLAYER EXCLUSIVE ADIDAS SHOE SELLS OUT IN LESS THAN AN HOUR ONLINE

The initiative, which was limited to Adidas outlets in Israel, included posters and videos featuring 10 disabled athletes. The campaign was focused on the company's single shoe service, showcasing athletes who require just one shoe due to amputations or accidents.

Veteran Shalev Biton, who lost in May 2021 during the conflict in Gaza, was featured in the advertisement. The Hebrew-language video did not mention Biton's army service or an explanation of how he lost his leg.

Criticism falsely claimed that Biton was involved in the recent fighting in Gaza, with anti-Israel activists accusing him of participating in "genocide." In reality, his accident occurred more than five years ago when an anti-tank missile fired from inside Gaza hit the military vehicle he was in on the Israeli side of the border. Fellow soldier Staff Sgt. Omer Tabib was killed during the action.

"Across the Middle East, Adidas has a long-standing commitment to the communities we serve, working alongside athletes, teams and sporting communities throughout the region as well as supporting people and communities in need through product donations," Adidas' statement continued.

"We will continue to listen, learn and work to ensure that our actions reflect the inclusive values we stand for."

Biton, who returned to running with a prosthetic limb, took to social media amid the intense wave of backlash he received online following the advertisement.

"Been hit by an absolutely insane wave of hatred and reports from all over the world," Biton wrote to his Instagram followers, per The Jerusalem Post. "Some of the biggest pro-Palestinian pages in the world, with millions of followers and millions of likes and shares, have been posting about me again and again, and the abuse and reports just don’t stop," he continued.

The recent war in Gaza began in October 2023.

item.title: SEC accuses LSU of letting Lane Kiffin run wild as expulsion vote coming Thursday in explosive court filing
item.description: SEC officials will hold a special meeting Thursday to consider expelling LSU over what they call a complete lack of institutional control over Lane Kiffin.
item.content:encoded:
The SEC filed an amended complaint Tuesday morning in an Alabama federal court, indicating that the conference is seriously considering drastic action against LSU.

After what unfolded last week in a Louisiana district court, it has become clear that the fight launched by LSU over the potential rostering of athletes with NFL experience has not gone over well with officials inside SEC headquarters.

Last Thursday, while SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey took the stand in a Baton Rouge courtroom, the conference filed a federal lawsuit against LSU, head coach Lane Kiffin and athletic department staffers. The lawsuit argued that the school was preventing SEC officials from exercising their First Amendment rights to govern the conference.

LSU HOLDS OFF ON ADDING PLAYERS WITH NFL TIES AS SEC LAWSUIT LOOMS OVER PROGRAM, LANE KIFFIN

Sankey testified for more than three hours, a hearing OutKick attended, and the gamesmanship quickly disappeared. Behind the scenes, the SEC was preparing to take action against LSU over a fiasco that had placed the conference and its leadership at the center of what was viewed as an embarrassing situation in Birmingham.

"The SEC does not bring this action to declare any student-athlete ineligible or to prevent any student-athlete from participating in any athletic competition. This action is directed solely at the state actors who have violated, continue to violate, and threaten to further violate the SEC’s rights under the First Amendment," the complaint noted.

LSU MIGHT HAVE TO SUE THE SEC IF THIS LEGAL WAR IS EXPEDITED, WHILE DABO SWINNEY IS STAYING IN HIS 'LANE'

The fight is now moving beyond the courtroom.

On Thursday, SEC officials will hold a special meeting to determine whether LSU could face expulsion from the conference. The meeting centers on concerns that school officials have lost control of Kiffin and the football program.

In the filing, SEC presidents and chancellors made it clear during a Sept. 4 meeting that they feel as though LSU has let Lane Kiffin run the football program however he wants, without guidance from the athletic department.

"Expressed great concern that Defendants Rousse and Ausberry have no meaningful control over Defendant Kiffin or the football program at LSU...The consensus at the September 4 meeting was and continues to be that LSU’s demonstrated lack of institutional control at the University level—including complete lack of control over Defendant Kiffin’s actions."

Simply put, the SEC feels as though the comments made by Kiffin over the past few weeks regarding this matter go against conference rules, and they feel as though the LSU athletic department has allowed Kiffin to run the football program without pressure from his own bosses.

Will this actually take place?

That's up to the member institutions, though the likelihood of the SEC expelling LSU from the conference feels pretty slim in the grand scheme of things.

But, in their updated filing on Tuesday, the SEC made it clear that they have the power to expel LSU from the conference, if enough votes are cast in favor of the move.

"Membership of a member may be terminated involuntarily at a meeting of the Chief Executive Officers. A vote of at least two-thirds of all the Chief Executive Officers is required to terminate membership. Any motion to terminate membership shall specify the effective date of the proposed termination," the complaint notes.

Right now, we are witnessing a fight between one of the biggest schools in the conference, and SEC members who are tired of being made fools of by Kiffin.

LSU'S LANE KIFFIN ADMITS HE LET TIGER STADIUM WEATHER DELAY DRAG ON IN ORDER TO HURT CLEMSON

And, when Sankey took the stand last week inside a Baton Rouge courthouse, the stakes were raised in this matter to the point where the SEC has now made it clear that they are not going to just brush this under the table because LSU decided not to roster players like Dae'Quan Wright this past weekend.

This has obviously ruffled plenty of feathers, and Kiffin's comments during the Clemson game this past weekend regarding how much worse the outcome could have been if LSU had been able to roster pro players were seen as the school having zero control over its head coach.

LSU’S LANE KIFFIN FIRES BACK AT NFL RETURNEE BACKLASH: BLAME THE NCAA, NOT US FOR RECRUITING PRO ATHLETES

"Defendant Kiffin’s statements and position, along with the numerous other statements and actions by Defendants alleged herein, stand in sharp contrast to the silence by the President and Athletic Director of LSU after Defendant Rousse voted for the Policy Statement on August 25, 2026," the SEC noted in its amended complaint.

"And they confirm the lack of institutional control over the athletics program at LSU that is required by Article 6 of the SEC Constitution and by the remaining provisions of the Constitution and Bylaws referenced above."

Not only is the SEC under the impression that LSU is allowing Lane Kiffin to run his football program without guidance from school officials, they see this as a slap in the face to the rules enacted regarding pro-athletes coming back to college.

"In light of the recalcitrance, lack of institutional control, and serious harm caused by the statements and conduct of LSU, the 15 SEC CEOs (other than LSU) have informally told the Commissioner (and President Plowman has directed the Commissioner) to issue a notice of the Special Meeting to be conducted on September 10, 2026, to consider the termination of LSU’s membership in the SEC, whether LSU renounces its intention to roster and play professional players on its football team, or not."

The SEC is obviously past the point of frustration with Lane Kiffin, and now we're about to find out how serious they are regarding penalties against the school in which they feel has embarrassed them enough.

Just when you thought the college football season would provide us an opportunity to talk about other things taking place outside a courtroom, the SEC decided to drop a public hammer on Tuesday.

Will they actually do it? Probably not, but they clearly want to embarrass LSU in the process.

item.title: FIBA Women's World Cup players' hotel evacuated after fire breaks out ahead of high-stakes final stage
item.description: A fire in a neighboring parking facility forced Women's Basketball World Cup teams out of their Berlin hotel for the second time in three days.
item.content:encoded:
Women’s Basketball World Cup teams were forced to evacuate their Berlin hotel early Tuesday morning for the second time in three days, after a fire started in a neighboring parking facility.

FIBA said the alarm went off at 9:06 a.m. local time. The teams followed standard safety procedures and assembled outside before returning to their rooms at 9:27 a.m.

"Following a thorough inspection, it was confirmed that the alarm was activated due to the start of a fire in the garbage room located in the underground basement of a neighbouring parking facility," FIBA said in a statement.

"The Police are currently investigating the exact circumstances surrounding the incident."

The U.S. team was not affected because the Americans are staying at a different hotel from the rest of the tournament field.

WNBA STAR WILL MISS PLAYING IN FIBA WORLD CUP AFTER HER PASSPORT GOES MISSING IN THE MAIL

The incident came two days after an alarm forced players and coaches out of the same hotel at approximately 2 a.m. Sunday. That evacuation lasted about an hour and disrupted the sleep of teams scheduled to play later that day.

FIBA said Tuesday that the first alarm "was due to steam in the kitchen during its cleaning." Australia coach Sandy Brondello had previously said she was told someone activated an emergency alarm in an elevator, according to The Associated Press.

THE PREDOMINANT BASKETBALL DYNASTY ON EARTH IS AT STAKE AS AMERICA'S EYES TURN TO CAITLIN CLARK'S ROLE

Tuesday’s evacuation occurred on the opening day of the knockout stage. Hungary and Japan were scheduled to play the first qualification game, followed by host Germany against South Korea. The winners will advance to face the U.S. and Belgium, respectively, in Thursday’s quarterfinals.

FIBA did not report any injuries or changes to the tournament schedule.

"The safety of all participants remains FIBA’s priority and we are taking all measures to make sure that the teams are put in the best possible conditions to compete," the organization said.

item.title: Reid Detmers and his 182 strikeouts give the Los Angeles Angels an edge over Boston Red Sox
item.description: Reid Detmers and his 182 strikeouts give the Los Angeles Angels a starting pitcher edge over Patrick Sandoval and the Boston Red Sox tonight.
item.content:encoded:
For whatever reason, the betting gods have rained down their fury on me over the past few days. I have been losing virtually every bet that I have placed. College football started, and I had the worst weekend I've ever had betting on the sport. I bet big on the Blue Jays yesterday and Dylan Cease let me down. Not exactly what I am looking for as a sports betting analyst. As always, the good news is that we get betting options daily, and we can get some of that money back on this one between the Angels and Red Sox.

The Los Angeles Angels are in the midst of yet another lost season. They will almost certainly finish as the worst team in their division, and potentially the worst team in baseball. Another 100-loss season is on the horizon unless they can win seven of their final 18 games. Considering they are winning only 38% of their games, it seems a bit unlikely that they will get the seven wins needed to avoid the 100-loss fate. The only good news is that this team is being sold, and perhaps new ownership will turn this franchise around.

The other good news is that they get another start from their staff Ace, Reid Detmers. It has been a very strong season from Detmers this year, with him going 4-8 for the year, posting a 3.44 ERA, and a 1.06 WHIP. He is also 10th in baseball with 182 strikeouts. Detmers has been worse on the road this season, but his numbers aren't terrible. His road ERA is 3.80, compared with 3.21 at home. He has been fantastic since the start of August, going 37 innings and allowing just six earned runs. One of his worst starts of the season came against Boston, where he allowed five earned runs over five innings.

The Boston Red Sox avoided a disaster season by becoming one of the hottest teams in baseball history. They have been extremely streaky over the past couple of months, winning a ton, then losing a few in a row. They've won their past five games, including the series opener yesterday. However, even this win streak saw them lose six of their previous eight games before starting this streak. And before that, they won five games in a row again. The team is currently 15 games above .500 and owners of the second Wild Card spot.

item.title: Iran-backed attacks threaten a second major oil chokepoint as new risk emerges for US consumers
item.description: Houthi missiles and drones struck Aramco facilities across Saudi Arabia, threatening to squeeze both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.
item.content:encoded:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck Saudi Arabia with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones Tuesday, hitting multiple energy targets, including the facilities of the world's largest oil company.

The attacks on Aramco, the state-owned national oil company of Saudi Arabia that produces 10 million barrels of oil per day, threaten to tighten pressure on a second critical oil route as the Middle East war continues to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Aramco notably supplies roughly 10% of the world's total oil demand. And attacks on its facilities raise the risk of higher oil, shipping and transportation costs that could hit U.S. consumers in coming months — just in time for the 2026 midterm elections.

IRAN CALLS ON HOUTHIS TO PREPARE TO CUT OFF RED SEA GATEWAY — CAN THE TERROR GROUP DO IT?

The attacks hit the southern Saudi Arabian cities of Jazan, Najran, Abha and Khamis Mushait, wounding 73 people and sparking fires at energy facilities and utilities that temporarily forced some operations to stop, according to Saudi officials. The Jazan site includes a refinery capable of processing roughly 400,000 barrels of crude per day, according to the Associated Press.

Tuesday's strikes land at a particularly vulnerable moment for global energy markets. With oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz sharply reduced, Saudi Arabia has redirected more crude toward the Red Sea — increasing the importance of the Bab el-Mandeb, where the Houthis have already threatened and attacked Saudi-linked shipping.

The Energy Information Administration estimates that just 4.9 million barrels of oil and petroleum liquids moved through Hormuz per day in the second quarter of 2026, down from 21.6 million barrels per day before the conflict. Before the conflict 20% of the world's oil moved through the consequential waterway.

Traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb, meanwhile, averaged 8.1 million barrels per day during the quarter as Saudi Arabia redirected more crude to bypass Hormuz amid ongoing conflict.

That creates a potentially costly vulnerability: renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure or commercial vessels could put pressure on two crucial oil routes at once, raising the risk of higher crude, shipping and transportation costs that could eventually reach U.S. consumers.

Brent crude was trading near $99 per barrel Tuesday.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Tuesday’s strikes, saying the group had used "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones" against Aramco facilities, the Jazan industrial zone and a Saudi air base, according to Xinhua.

RUBIO ACCUSES IRAN OF FLYING IRGC PERSONNEL INTO YEMEN AS HOUTHI THREAT ESCALATES

The Houthis said the operation was retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen and threatened "stronger and wider strikes" if Riyadh’s military campaign continues.

The escalation also comes with a warning already issued by President Donald Trump.

After the Houthis struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in July, Trump said the U.S. would hold Iran responsible if the group attacked ships again and threatened "major military punishment" against both Tehran and the Houthis.

"If they do this again, the U.S. will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves," Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.

The warning followed the Houthis’ announcement of a maritime blockade targeting Saudi Arabia and attacks on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea. The escalation sent Brent crude above $100 per barrel amid fears that disruption could spread from the Strait of Hormuz to the Bab el-Mandeb.

The latest strikes targeted Saudi territory and energy infrastructure rather than ships, leaving unclear whether the White House considers them to cross the line Trump drew in July. It creates a new test for the administration as Houthi attacks increasingly intersect with the wider conflict over Iran and regional energy supplies.

The Trump administration has previously authorized U.S. strikes against Houthi weapons and infrastructure in Yemen in response to attacks and threats against American forces and shipping. A White House report says Trump directed those actions to defend U.S. forces and protect American national-security interests.

The U.S. Maritime Administration also maintains an active advisory warning that the Houthis continue to pose a threat to commercial vessels in the southern Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb and the Gulf of Aden.

From November 2023 through October 2025, the Houthis carried out more than 100 attacks on commercial vessels affecting more than 60 nations, according to the MARAD advisory. The attacks forced major shipping companies to avoid the Red Sea and reroute vessels around the Cape of Good Hope, adding time to voyages and increasing fuel, freight and insurance costs.

The Houthis renewed that threat in July when they targeted Saudi oil tankers and threatened a blockade of Saudi shipping through the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia’s increased reliance on the route makes another sustained disruption potentially more consequential. The EIA says alternate routes used to bypass disrupted waterways are longer, more expensive and limited in capacity.

The latest strikes threaten to revive pressure on the Red Sea route just as the Iran conflict has made the Persian Gulf route more difficult to use. The Houthis may lack the capability to permanently close the Bab el-Mandeb, but repeated missile, drone or tanker attacks could still reduce traffic through the waterway if shipping companies determine the risks are too high.

Saudi Arabia condemned Tuesday’s strikes on civilian and economic assets and vowed to defend its territory. The Saudi-led coalition described the attacks as a "dangerous escalation" and said it would take measures to deter further attacks.

The immediate economic impact will depend on how quickly Saudi Arabia restores affected operations and whether commercial shipping continues moving through the Bab el-Mandeb.

The next test could be whether the Houthis again target tankers or other commercial vessels. Another attack could put greater pressure on a waterway carrying an increased share of Middle Eastern oil — while also testing Trump’s warning that renewed Houthi attacks on shipping would bring U.S. retaliation against both the group and Iran.

In an interview discussing his rumored 2028 presidential run, California Gov. Gavin Newsom asserted that the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), especially when it comes to universal healthcare, climate change and moving away from fossil fuel usage.

During an interview with "PBS NewsHour," Newsom was questioned about what recent democratic socialist victories across the country mean for the Democratic Party.

"If you have these candidates and this platform that is clearly animating the base, energizing turnout, should more of those ideas be worked into the broader Democratic platform?" Newsom was asked.

The interviewer pressed Newsom further, saying, "There seems to be some distance between [Democratic] leadership and those DSA candidates."

"But, not the ideas," Newsom responded.

"I believe in universal healthcare, and I believe in Medicare for All, the party does overwhelmingly," he said. "And so, if it’s about more money in your pocket, lowering costs, getting money out of politics, if it’s about Medicare for All, I think we’re pretty aligned."

He added, "It’s about recognizing that we’ve got a planet that is getting hotter and drier and that we’ve got to address the issue of climate change, we want energy security, and we want to move off fossil fuels. That’s a DSA position, that’s a mainstream position within the Democratic Party."

Newsom dismissed worry about democratic socialist influence in American politics, saying, "I think in many ways, it’s just a label … it’s just such a familiar label to me, we call them progressives."

NEWSOM HIT WITH LAWSUIT THREAT AS WHISTLEBLOWER BEGS TRUMP FOR HELP WITH ‘MONUMENTAL’ FRAUD SCANDAL

"Maybe it's just because I’m from California and I think it’s healthy … I’m not consumed by this," the governor continued, adding that the DSA’s ideas reflect "aspects and component parts of our party that we’ve always had, and it’s a healthy dialectic within the party."

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom’s office for additional comment. Fox News Digital also reached out to the DSA and to the Democratic National Committee for comment.

The DSA is the pre-eminent socialist political group in the U.S. This year, the group rolled out an updated platform that includes eliminating the Senate and replacing the president and the Supreme Court with an executive and judiciary chosen by Congress. Additionally, the updated platform includes amnesty for all immigrants and defunding the Department of War.

JENNIFER SIEBEL NEWSOM DODGES QUESTION ON HUSBAND GAVIN'S PRESIDENTIAL ASPIRATIONS

This is in addition to the DSA’s already existing policy platform, which calls for an "immediate end to all deportations," free migration between countries without restrictive immigration controls, and "extending full voting rights to people with criminal convictions and noncitizens."

Once considered a fringe movement on the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, the DSA has been gaining relevance, with several of its members toppling longtime establishment party figures. This has prompted many to speculate that the DSA represents the Democratic Party’s future.

As car horns honk, Cruz grabs the girl, pulling her backwards as they both tumble safely to the ground in the lane closest to the store while the mini van screeches to a halt in the middle lane.

item.title: Trump posthumously awards Medal of Freedom to 9/11's 'man in red bandana'
item.description: President Donald Trump awards the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously to Welles Crowther, the heroic "man in the red bandana" who saved up to 18 lives during the September 11 attacks.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump honored deceased volunteer firefighter Welles Crowther – also known as the "man in the red bandana" – with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday. 

Speaking during Tunnel to Towers' "Steel Across America" event in Washington, D.C. on Tuesday, President Donald Trump praised Crowther, whose actions during 9/11 saved up to 18 people's lives, sparking nationwide admiration and a series of documentary features on his bravery. 

"Today we also remember another hero of 9/11. After the plane hit the south tower, a group of people on the 78th floor were trapped with broken bones, charred skin and eyes and lungs filled with black smoke. Death was all about them. It was certain they were sure they were going to die. Then suddenly a rescuer appeared. They call him the man in the red bandana. Have you heard that term? The man in the red bandana has become more famous than me. I don't like it. Very unhappy. But he's become much more famous than me," Trump joked. 

"He's the man in the red bandana. He had found the only stairwell that barely survived. The stairwells were all knocked down. You couldn't get by. Impassable. He found an opening in one of the stairwells, and the impact was so great there was no other way down but this one little opening, this one little hole. And [he] traveled down from the 104th floor to look for those trapped and dying," Trump continued.

First responders honor World Trade Center beam arriving at Boston fallen heroes memorial

"When he heard cries for help on the 78th floor, he began extinguishing the fires, blocking the exit, directing survivors who could walk, of which there weren't that many. He helped them out physically. They literally pulled him out toward the only working stairwell and carried those who couldn't walk. And he just did things that people said were not even imaginable because they knew they were dead. They said, 'we're goners.' One guy was screaming, 'we're goners! We're goners!' He didn't know those he helped and, nor who would have known, but he willingly made all of these trips up and down, up and down, up and down, over and over again, saving life after life," Trump added.

Rutgers unveils special uniforms to honor 37 alumni killed in September 11 attacks

"That rescuer was a 24-year-old equities trader and volunteer firefighter from Rockland County named Welles Crowther. And Welles' father, also a firefighter, great firefighter, had given him that bandana as a very special tribute when he was a boy. He probably knew something about his son. When asked why he always kept it, Welles replied 'with this red bandana, I'm going to change the world. I'm going to change the world with this bandana.' Little did he know, on September 11th Welles saved many, many people before losing his own life in the South Tower lobby. When the building came down, he was in the lobby and that building came down, thousands of tons of steel," Trump said.

"Today, in honor of his incredible bravery and all of the other countless unknown acts of heroism that day, it is my privilege to award the very special, the highest honor that we give, the highest civilian honor, the Presidential Medal of Freedom. We want to award that to Welles and the Welles family. Welles is up there looking down at his mom and his sister, his family," Trump said. 

Trump was speaking during the Tunnel to Towers' "Steel Across America" event, in which the organization takes a 16,900 lb steel beam that came from the World Trade Center's South Tower across the country. 

The president also invited Crowther's mother on stage to speak about her son after reminding the crowd that he had promised her earlier to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, to her son. 

FRANK SILLER: 'I love you, brother' -- the 9/11 loss that inspired a mission of service

"That Welles' light still shines brilliantly today, even after 25 years, is testament to his legacy of courage, compassion and love for humanity that continues to inspire and uplift others," Alison Crowther said. 

"Welles, however, would not have been able to do what he did as effectively on 9/11 if it had not been for the training and experience he gained as a member of Empire Hook and Ladder Company Number one of Upper Nyack. Empire is a volunteer company and the members are fully trained firefighters. They have other jobs and responsibilities, businesses to run and their own families. But when the alarm goes off at any time, day or night, they respond to the call to save life and property. This is a calling. And Welles – following in the footsteps of his father, Jefferson – joined Empire at the age of 16. He was no longer an equities trader on 9/11, he was a firefighter," she said.

NON-CITIZEN POLICE OFFICERS APPROVED AFTER DEM SAYS ICE 'INVASION' 'SENDS A MESSAGE'

item.title: Lane Kiffin urges LSU fans to show up for Louisiana Tech game, tells them to start drinking at 7AM
item.description: Lane Kiffin challenged LSU fans to start drinking at 7 a.m. and pack Death Valley for Saturday's Louisiana Tech game after the Clemson blowout.
item.content:encoded:
You can't drink all day if you don't start first thing in the morning. That's not verbatim the message LSU head coach Lane Kiffin is sending his school's fanbase heading into Week 2 of the season, but it's one he's implying.

Fresh off a 51-10 thrashing of Clemson to open up the Kiffin tenure in Baton Rouge, the Tigers welcome Louisiana Tech to town on Saturday evening. The atmosphere with the Bulldogs in town will pale in comparison to what was witnessed in Death Valley for the season opener against the Tigers.

Kiffin knows that, but it isn't stopping him from challenging the fanbase to show up and show out.

LSU HAD A REVIVAL, CLEMSON WAS AT A FUNERAL: LANE KIFFIN’S DEBUT SENDS A LOUD MESSAGE TO COLLEGE FOOTBALL

"Don’t let the opponent dictate how you are a fan. We challenge our players to do that, so, the fans, too," Kiffin told reporters on Monday. "If you’ve got to have a mock Saturday or put up a stage of 'College GameDay' — whatever it is. Come out here early; come out here and start drinking at 7:00 a.m.."

"Everything’s got to be the same as last Saturday," he continued. "I challenge our fans the same thing. The fans were electric. The whole walk, the beginning of the game, the first quarter – you could feel it coming down on the opponent. People who have been here a long time, they said it was the loudest, intense feelings they felt ever."

Kiffin urging fans to come and support his team against a not-so-flashy opponent is nothing new, nor is it a tactic exclusive to him. The 51-year-old coach issued the same sort of statements during his tenure at Ole Miss when the Rebels welcomed smaller, out-of-conference opponents to Oxford.

Most other coaches of Power Four programs face the same challenge of having fans show up – which translates to spending their money – at games that aren't exactly circled on the calendar.

LSU'S LANE KIFFIN ADMITS HE LET TIGER STADIUM WEATHER DELAY DRAG ON IN ORDER TO HURT CLEMSON

Louisiana Tech certainly falls into that category for much of the LSU fanbase, with the contest sandwiched between the home opener against Clemson, which can only be described as a dominant party, and the Tigers' trip to Ole Miss next week in what is undoubtedly one of the most highly anticipated games of the college football season.

As for Kiffin's joke about LSU fans pouring a cocktail at 7 a.m. before the Tigers kick off at 6:30 p.m. on Saturday against Louisiana Tech, that's a challenge plenty of fans in Baton Rouge will accept.

item.title: Britain’s dramatic crackdown on Israeli settlements sparks fierce response as US blowback looms

The United Kingdom unveiled sweeping new measures targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, triggering an immediate diplomatic rupture with Israel and a sharp warning from a senior Trump administration official.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar announced Tuesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s approval, that Israel would close the British Consulate in Jerusalem and impose a series of countermeasures in response to the U.K. sanctions.

The Israeli measures also include removing British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat, ending British activities training Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank and denying entry to 12 British elected officials and other British nationals whom Israel accused of antisemitic or anti-Israel activity.

UK MOVES TO SANCTION ISRAELI SETTLEMENTS AS PM BURNHAM RISKS CLASH WITH TRUMP: REPORT

"Measures against Israel will not go unanswered," Sa’ar said. "Whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region."

The escalation came hours after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament that Britain would ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements, target companies and individuals facilitating settlement expansion, and refuse licenses for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation.

The move is part of a coordinated push with France, Canada and other European partners amid what the governments described Tuesday as "unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion" in the West Bank, including Israel’s E1 project, which they argue threatens the viability of a future Palestinian state. The measures come just weeks before world leaders gather for the U.N. General Assembly in New York and less than two months before Israel’s Oct. 27 election, adding diplomatic and political stakes to an already strained relationship between Israel and several of its traditional Western allies.

At the same time, the foreign ministers recognized Israel’s "legitimate security interests" and reiterated their condemnation of Hamas’ Oct. 7 terrorist attack, which they described as "the worst antisemitic massacre since the Holocaust." They said their objective remained a two-state solution allowing Israel and "a sovereign, democratic and viable Palestinian state" to live side by side in peace and security.

UK DEFENSE SHORTFALLS HIGHLIGHTED AS BRITAIN AVOIDS IRAN OFFENSIVE ROLE AMID TRUMP CRITICISM

The timing has also become a political issue inside Britain. An unnamed Labor MP told The Telegraph that Prime Minister Andy Burnham had faced pressure from colleagues worried about Gaza-related campaigning and losing seats to the Greens, while Israeli officials have accused London of trying to influence Israel’s election — claims the British government rejects as it frames the measures as an effort to preserve the two-state solution.

"Today, I announce that the official view of the British government is that the occupation is unlawful," Miliband told lawmakers Tuesday.

Miliband opened the statement by describing himself as a "proud British Jew" with "the deepest gratitude to the State of Israel," recalling how his grandmother found refuge there after losing her husband and 60 other family members at the hands of the Nazis.

He stressed that the measures were aimed at settlements rather than Israel itself.

"The sanctions regime will target illegal settlement and settlement expansion. Not Israel," Miliband said, adding that Britain would continue to support trade with Israel inside the Green Line and that he "wholeheartedly" opposed the broader Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement.

Miliband also condemned rising antisemitism in Britain, saying, "Holding British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, plain and simple."

He reaffirmed Israel’s right to defend itself against terrorism, called for Hamas to disarm and dismantle its terrorist infrastructure under the U.S. -led 20-point Gaza plan, and announced sanctions against Hezbollah financing institution Al-Qard Al-Hassan. He also said Britain was reimposing major economic sanctions on Iran and would continue security cooperation with Israel against shared threats.

The measures drew immediate criticism from U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who warned in an interview with BBC World Service Newsday that Britain could face economic repercussions in the United States.

ISRAELI OFFICIAL SAYS EU SANCTIONS REVEAL ANTISEMITISM HIDING BEHIND 'SOCIALLY ACCEPTABLE MASK'

"I think without a doubt there will be," Huckabee said when asked whether the U.K. should expect consequences.

Huckabee pointed to Florida and other states with anti-boycott laws, arguing that British companies could face restrictions on doing business there.

"If the Brits do something like this with a partner, Israel, then they will not be able to do business in Florida," he said, warning of a "huge economic impact on British businesses."

He also challenged Britain’s policy on substantive grounds, arguing that Israel is permitted under the Oslo agreements to build communities in Area C and predicting that the sanctions would have "a very negative effect that does not meet whatever goal maybe that the Brits have."

In a separate portion of the BBC interview, Huckabee said, "I feel like that it's a discrimination against the Israeli government. It's a discrimination against the Jewish people. And I don't understand the rationale."

The Trump administration also made clear Tuesday that Washington would not join the coordinated sanctions push. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States does not want to see "anything destabilizing" in the West Bank, but said Washington would not follow Britain, France and Canada in blocking imports from Israeli settlements, according to Reuters.

IS ISRAEL REALLY ISOLATED? POLLS AND DIPLOMACY POINT IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS

Sa’ar also accused London of interfering in Israel’s election campaign and said the settlement sanctions were driven by domestic British politics ahead of the Labor Party conference.

"The British move is morally distorted and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process," he said.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Britain’s move a "grave miscalculation" Tuesday and argued that it amounted to "gross interference" in Israel’s upcoming election, according to a statement from his office.

Nitsana Darshan-Leitner, president and founder of the Tel Aviv-based Shurat HaDin-Israel Law Center, also criticized the measures, arguing that the economic impact would be limited while the political consequences could be significant.

"These sanctions are not serious economic policy; they are political theater staged at Israel’s expense," Darshan-Leitner told Fox News Digital. She disputed Britain’s legal characterization of the territory, saying, "The territories are disputed, not sovereign Palestinian land, and their future must be negotiated by the parties under the Oslo framework."

Darshan-Leitner also argued that because little of the roughly $8 billion in annual U.K.-Israel trade originates in West Bank settlements, the measures would have little direct economic effect while potentially influencing Israel’s political debate ahead of elections.

Miliband, however, argued that failing to act would allow continued settlement expansion to destroy the possibility of a two-state solution. He focused particularly on Israel’s E1 project east of Jerusalem, which Britain and numerous other governments say threatens the territorial viability of a future Palestinian state.

Sa'ar rejected Britain’s position that the E1 settlement project threatens the viability of a future Palestinian state.

UK PINS STRING OF ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ON IRAN-LINKED GROUP, BANS IRGC

The policy has also exposed divisions within Britain.

Conservative lawmaker Tom Tugendhat acknowledged in Parliament that illegal settlements were wrong and that some settlers had committed "outrageous abuses" against Palestinians, but argued that the government’s response risked hurting ordinary Israelis and Palestinians.

"What we reject here is not the intent, but the performative politics," Tugendhat said, warning against acting without sufficiently broad international support.

Miliband rejected arguments that the measures were intended to isolate Israel.

"Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the U.K. has unshakable bonds," he said. "Our argument is with the conduct of its government."

item.title: From power failures to moral victories, Monday night couldn't have gone much worse for Florida State fans
item.description: Florida State's Labor Day loss to SMU stretched college football beyond Saturday, but the close score at Doak Campbell Stadium may save Mike Norvell.
item.content:encoded:
Week one of the college football season is always an absolute blast, mainly because instead of a lone Saturday of action, your weekend of football watching gets stretched to three magical days over the holiday weekend.

One of the highlights of every week one is always the standalone game on Labor Day night, but unfortunately for Florida State fans, their Seminoles were the ones tasked with entertaining a football hungry public.

The game itself was somewhat entertaining and had plenty of drama, but we will discuss that here in a bit.

SEC TEAMS WENT 16-0 IN WEEK 1, IS THE CONFERENCE BACK ON TOP OF COLLEGE FOOTBALL WORLD?

By now, everyone is aware of the power outage that took place at Doak Campbell Stadium on Monday night.

If you were tuning in to watch Florida State take on SMU, you were likely greeted with a mostly dark stadium and a bunch of reporters sitting around a desk trying desperately to fill air time.

MANY ARE MAKING THE ARGUMENT THAT JORDAN TRAVIS WAS THE GREATEST COLLEGE QB OF ALL TIME, AND THEY AREN'T WRONG

The broadcast crew for ESPN did an admirable job with what they were given, but make no mistake about it, this was a national embarrassment for a program that has been full of them these past 24 months.

Unfortunately, the power failure wasn't even the worst part of last night's "Debacle at Doak."

FROM FSU TO DAN MULLEN, HERE ARE THREE 'OVERREACTIONS' FROM WEEK ZERO OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON

Sure, it was fun for fans of every other team to sit back on their couches, pointing and laughing at FSU's incompetence with regard to paying their electric bill, but once the game started, it was a lot closer than anyone was willing to predict in the lead up.

And a close game late into the fourth quarter is precisely what Noles fans DID NOT want to happen.

To be clear, SMU dominated this game.

The Mustangs marched the ball up and down the field seemingly at will, racking up nearly 600 yards of total offense and going 8-for-14 on third down, but it almost seemed like they were trying to give this game away to the Seminoles.

WHICH HEAD COACH'S SEAT IS HOTTER HEADING INTO 2026 SEASON: SHANE BEAMER OR MIKE NORVELL?

And FSU simply would not take it.

A game in which SMU outgained Florida State by 261 yards came down to the final possession, which presents a nightmare scenario for any Seminole supporter looking to offload head coach Mike Norvell's albatross of a contract.

The Noles are 1-1 and have a "competitive" game against a top-25 opponent under their belts, so anyone hoping for an exit strategy with their beleaguered head coach might be in for a rude awakening.

It would have been better to get blown out on national television, especially with the pregame power outage.

A close loss that came down to the last few seconds gives Norvell a sliver of hope, which as we all know is poison.

Don't get me wrong, there were plenty of other embarrassing moments for the Noles that represented a microcosm of the Norvell era, like this joker who dribbled an imaginary basketball on third and ten right before his defense gave up a 30 yard completion.

Seminole fans are in football purgatory right now.

There doesn't seem to be an end in sight, and a close loss to a College Football Playoff hopeful was basically the equivalent to God adding another million tons of sand to their hourglass of suffering.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

The money will be raised to cut ties with Norvell eventually, but $51 million is a big chunk of change, and the powers that be will be looking for every reason not to pay it until that number comes down.

If you're an FSU supporter, you should be praying that this season goes off the rails, because 7-5 with close losses to teams like SMU will only prolong the inevitable.

It's time to rip the Band-Aid off, but Norvell keeps supergluing it to Chief Osceola's skin.

item.title: Colorado TPUSA chapter enrollment 'flat' after elderly supporter was stricken by student with Taco Bell cup
item.description: Video captured the chaos after Fort Lewis College approved a Turning Point USA chapter, but nearly a year later, membership remains stagnant.
item.content:encoded:
Enrollment at the Turning Point USA (TPUSA) chapter at Fort Lewis College in Durango, Colorado, remains flat due to students’ fears of retaliation, according to chapter leaders and local supporters. The stagnation comes nearly a year after the campus group's registration sparked intense pushback from the surrounding community and student body.

"It's definitely been flat, I would say," Rachel Cook, vice president of the Fort Lewis College chapter, told Fox News Digital.

Cook’s comments come nearly a year after the student government's decision to recognize the chapter touched off severe turmoil on campus — much of which was captured on video and obtained by Fox News Digital.

ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

One video showed a student being detained by campus police after striking 66-year-old local resident David Peters with a Taco Bell cup outside the student senate chambers.

Peters, former chair of the La Plata County GOP and a retired Chevron executive, reflected on the incident and its lingering effect on the student group.

"Their membership has been essentially flat. The issue is that a lot of students are reluctant to join the chapter for fear of retaliation," Peters said. "And their fears are well-founded. There have been some members who have received anonymous death threats."

Cook echoed those safety concerns. 

"One of the main things is that students have said they are hesitant to join because of their personal safety. A lot of our officers have been getting threats and being harassed," she said.

UC BERKELEY SUED FOR ALLEGEDLY STONEWALLING PROBE INTO VIOLENT AMBUSH AT TPUSA ROB SCHNEIDER EVENT

The tensions at Fort Lewis College unfolded amid a national surge in interest for TPUSA campus chapters. Following the September 10, 2025, assassination of TPUSA co-founder Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University, the conservative organization reported receiving more than 120,000 inquiries from students seeking to establish local chapters.

At Fort Lewis College, then-senior Jonah Flynn led the effort to establish a presence on campus. Although the Associated Students of Fort Lewis College (ASFLC) initially rejected Flynn’s proposal, the student government ultimately reversed course and voted to approve the group during an emergency session.

The vote prompted immediate outrage from anti-TPUSA spectators waiting outside the meeting room.

According to a Fort Lewis College campus police report, approximately 70 people attended the high-tension meeting. As attendees spilled out into the lobby, an argument broke out between attendees holding opposing views.

The police report states that Peters approached a student who was "booing and yelling" while holding his phone about a foot away to record. The student — identified in police records as Megan Elizabeth Hope Mollett (who goes by Nova and uses they/them pronouns) — struck Peters' phone and hand with an empty Taco Bell cup.

NEWLY LAUNCHED TPUSA CHAPTER CAUSES UPROAR AT MICHIGAN HIGH SCHOOL BEFORE FIRST MEETING

Officers intervened immediately, separating the pair and detaining Mollett. While the incident was documented as harassment, police released Mollett with a warning after Peters declined to press criminal charges, though he requested that the university take internal disciplinary action.

Reflecting on the fallout nearly a year later, Peters noted that the climate on campus remains hostile.

During the same post-vote protest, David Kozak, a former anthropology professor at the college, was captured on video flipping off the camera and shouting at TPUSA supporters.

"Go on, fascists," Kozak shouted. "Go on, Nazi lovers... C’mon, Nazis!"

A spokesperson for Fort Lewis College confirmed to Fox News Digital that Kozak has since retired from the university.

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

The ongoing hostility comes as political violence remains a growing concern across the country following Kirk's assassination. Authorities cited political motivation in the shooting, pointing to evidence including ammunition allegedly engraved with political slogans, highlighting concerns over how inflammatory rhetoric is translating into real-world violence.

Fort Lewis College did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment regarding Cook's and Peters' claims.

item.title: Bryan Kohberger's bid to oust judge and undo guilty plea moves forward with new court date set
item.description: Bryan Kohberger's new lawyers challenge Judge Steven Hippler's impartiality as the convicted Idaho murders killer fights to undo his guilty plea.
item.content:encoded:
Convicted Idaho student murderer Bryan Kohberger will return to court on Oct. 15 for a hearing on his motion to remove Judge Steven Hippler from his case as he seeks to undo his guilty plea through a process known as post-conviction relief.

Kohberger, 31, filed a handwritten petition in July, telling the court he had ineffective counsel, that his guilty plea was "not knowingly or voluntarily entered because it was induced by unkept promises" and that it was "not voluntarily entered because of threats asserted by petitioner's (Kohberger's) legal counsel."

The court appointed attorney Greg Rauch, of Moscow, Idaho, and private defense lawyer Jason Goldman, of New York, later joined Kohberger's new legal team.

BRYAN KOHBERGER APPOINTED NEW LAWYER AFTER IDAHO MURDERS CASE COSTS TAXPAYERS OVER $8 MILLION

His new lawyers are expected to file an amended petition by Nov. 13 — four years to the day after the murders.

"We think the [amended petition] and evidentiary hearing will naturally address some of the outstanding and unanswered questions," Goldman told Fox News Digital last week. "That said, the main priority right now is to scrutinize the constitutional issues surrounding Bryan's plea."

BRYAN KOHBERGER’S 2027 HEARING IS NOT GUARANTEED AS IDAHO SEEKS QUICK DISMISSAL

Kohberger pleaded guilty on July 2, 2025, to four counts of first-degree murder and a burglary charge for the stabbing deaths of 21-year-olds Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves as well as 20-year-olds Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin.

On July 23, 2025, Hippler sentenced him to four consecutive terms of life in prison without the possibility of parole, plus another 10 years, as part of a plea deal in which Kohberger avoided the death penalty.

Rauch filed a 22-page motion to have the judge disqualified on Aug. 27, questioning Hippler's impartiality after he declined to give Kohberger's former defense team more time when they said they were not finished with discovery as the expected trial date approached last year.

Kohberger pleaded guilty weeks before it would have taken place. Rauch also took issue with some of the language Hippler used to describe his client at sentencing: "someone in whom the Court could identify nothing remaining that was 'good or intrinsically human.'"

In the prosecution's fight against his petition for post-conviction relief, Deputy Latah County Prosecuting Attorney Keith Scholl asked for the transcripts from both hearings, in which Kohberger admitted guilt and affirmed he was entering his plea knowingly and under no duress.

In a separate order last week, Hippler gave Kohberger's lawyers until Sept. 10 to explain why the court should seal a supplemental filing attached to their motion to disqualify him from the case.

They've also been ordered to share the confidential filing with the Latah County Prosecutor's office. It has not been made public and will remain sealed at least until the deadline — likely longer after a justification is given.

item.title: Remembering Charlie Kirk: Turning Point USA's Andrew Kolvet reflects on conservative group's challenging year
item.description: Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet reveals how Erika Kirk's leadership prevented the organization from unraveling after Charlie Kirk's death.
item.content:encoded:
One year ago this week, Turning Point USA founder and conservative icon Charlie Kirk was assassinated while speaking at Utah Valley University.

As the anniversary approaches, his closest allies are still grappling with the tragedy after losing their friend and leader in the prime of his life.

Andrew Kolvet, the spokesman for Turning Point USA and a close friend of Kirk's, called the past year "the most challenging year of my life."

"Not only did we live through the tragedy of losing Charlie in such a public, horrific way, but we've had to navigate the months afterwards, and try and pick up the pieces and keep charging forward, because I think there would have been a temptation for anybody to just be mired in grief and go into the fetal position after something like that happened. But we also understood that Charlie meant so much to so many people that we had to push forward and keep going," Kolvet told Fox News Digital.

TYLER ROBINSON TO FACE TRIAL IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION AS JUDGE KEEPS DEATH PENALTY ON TABLE

Kolvet, who first met Kirk in 2017 and began working for him in 2018, said he didn't expect a cottage industry of conspiracy theories to emerge from Kirk's murder, but he said he also didn't expect that stories from all over the country from people whose lives Kirk impacted would continue flooding in nearly a year later.

Kolvet recounted the story of an Indiana student and high school Turning Point chapter president who clashed with a mother while handing out bracelets.

"And she was like, 'You know, Charlie taught me how to stand up for myself and I won't back down. And I'm here because I was inspired to get involved by Charlie, his life and his death, and I won't back down,'" Kolvet said.

He continued, "And to see that kind of grit, like a happy warrior from our students and to see their enthusiasm and their willingness to stay engaged, stay fighting — all of those things have been truly remarkable for me to witness and not just witness from afar, hear anecdotes, but to hear their stories personally, for them to come up to me and tell me about it, come on the show and tell us about it has been really amazing."

ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

Kolvet credited Turning Point USA's continued success over the past year to Erika Kirk, Charlie Kirk's widow, who was appointed CEO of the group following his assassination, a succession plan Kolvet said Charlie had previously expressed in the event of his untimely death.

"The fact that she stepped into that very difficult role in the time and the way and the manner in which she did was so incredibly important, because if you don't know the inner workings of Turning Point, you don't know the way that it's set up, and you don't know all the individual personalities, I'm of the opinion that had she not stepped in when she did and how she did, that you could have seen the unraveling of Turning Point completely," Kolvet said. 

"She was the one person that could step into that place and have the respect, the love, and the appreciation from all the different parts of the organization and organizations that could have brought everybody together and realized, hey, we're going to fight together, we're going to be together, we're going to rally around each other and make sure Charlie's mission continues to march forward. And she was uniquely the only one, I believe, that could've done that."

ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY

He touted an "almost 200% growth" in Club American chapters in high schools with over 3,500 across the country and over 1,500 Turning Point college chapters, adding that when he was alive Charlie Kirk believed 1,000 would be the max. 

Kolvet also pointed to the spike in church partnerships, going from 4,000 to 12,000.

"Erica's done an incredible job driving success, being a visionary leader, stepping into the biggest shoes you can imagine... Charlie was a thousand percent right for entrusting her with this monumental task should something happen to him... And she stepped into an unimaginable situation and [did] an incredible job with that," Kolvet added.

item.title: Adam Carolla says Los Angeles went from a city no one left to a place residents flee for ‘anywhere’ else
item.description: The comedian reflected on how dramatically attitudes toward Los Angeles have changed during an appearance on the "Hanging Out with Sean Hannity" podcast.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Adam Carolla says Los Angeles has undergone a dramatic shift, arguing that the city went from a place where residents rarely left to one where they are now willing to move almost anywhere else.

"No one ever left LA," Carolla said on Tuesday's episode of the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "You would only leave LA if somebody's dad's company's headquarters moved for some reason or another, or you moved to Hawaii and you were just retiring."

"Now, people leave LA, and you go, 'Where are you going?' And they go, ‘Anywhere,'" he added.

BILLIONS IN TAXPAYER INCOME ARE LEAVING TWO ICONIC STATES — AS A NEW ECONOMIC MAP EMERGES

Carolla said leaving Los Angeles once seemed so unusual that he struggled to understand why anyone would move elsewhere in the country.

"When you're from LA, back in the day, if somebody said, 'We're moving to Tennessee...'" Carolla recalled. "I didn't know where Tennessee was. [I would say], 'What are you doing over there?'"

The comedian described the shift as a sign of broader problems in Los Angeles, arguing that some people are now leaving out of necessity.

"That's a bad sign," he said.

AMERICANS CONTINUE VOTING WITH THEIR FEET AS HIGH-TAX CITIES STRUGGLE TO RECOVER

"Because [the reason is] not 'our company is relocating,' or 'I'm retiring, and I'm moving to Hawaii.' It's 'I've just got to get out of here.'"

Carolla has repeatedly criticized California's Democratic leadership for similar reasons, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, as he has discussed the state’s homelessness crisis, wildfires and what he views as the state's broader decline.

He previously discussed leaving California himself, saying he planned to make the move after his children graduated from high school.
